details.title: The formula
details.body:
score  =  rise ÷ swing

rise    yearly % gain over the nine months
swing   yearly % up-and-down over the same days

Technology
78.3 ÷ 36.6 = 2.14

details.title: Reading it
details.body:
Above 1.00 the sector rose faster than it moved around. 0 is flat. Below 0 it fell.

Swing is the number each sector page calls its typical swing.

details.title: Which nine months
details.body:
5 November 2025 to 10 July 2026 — 168 trading days.

That window ends 21 trading days (one month) before the latest prices, and those 21 days are left out of every number on the screen. A share that jumped in the last few weeks often gives it back, so counting that jump would make a sector look stronger than it is.

details.title: What a sector is here
details.body:
Not a real fund — a list built from scratch.

Every US-listed company worth more than $2 billion is sorted by how much of it is bought and sold on an average day. The busiest 50 in each sector make the list.

All 50 count the same amount — 2% each — so one giant company cannot speak for the whole sector.

Communication has 48 instead of 50, because that is how many companies in it clear the size and trading bar.

details.title: The “x of 50 up” line
details.body:
Every company is scored on its own with the same arithmetic. That line counts how many finished above zero.

It matters because a sector can score well on the strength of a few names while most of it went nowhere. A high count means the whole sector moved; a low count means a handful carried it.

details.title: The real fund on each sector page
details.body:
Each sector page names the matching SPDR fund — XLK for technology, XLE for energy — and scores it over the identical nine months.

It will not match. That fund holds companies in proportion to their size and holds more than 50 of them; this basket holds the busiest 50 in equal amounts. It is there as a check that the sector is being read roughly right, not as the same thing.

details.title: What this does not tell you
details.body:
The 50 companies in each list are chosen using today's trading, and then their prices are read backwards over the past nine months. Companies that collapsed and dropped off the list are not in it. That makes the past look better than it was, and it means these are not returns anyone could have earned.

This ranks sectors as they stand today. It is not a trading record and it is not advice.

Put in the same order as the eleven real SPDR sector funds over these nine months, the two orderings line up at 0.83 — 1.00 would be identical, 0 would be unrelated.
